revisions_after_selection.change: Reframed the one-day closure as the public peak of a year-round Dior repair and restoration service, with the service launched and promoted before the first closure day.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The main risk named for C2 is that a single closure day reads as a stunt. A standing service gives the day a purpose and keeps repair and reuse visible beyond one date.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a clear invitation for clients to bring pieces they own, including pieces bought secondhand, with booking opened in advance and a simple handover after the day.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This widens the audience beyond first-hand buyers, reaches the secondhand audience C1 missed, and makes the offer practical rather than only theatrical.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a commitment to publish what is repaired each year (pieces mended, repair time, materials reused) and to open the ateliers' practices to scrutiny.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Supply-chain scrutiny could make the gesture look hypocritical. Measurable, transparent commitments let the brand answer criticism rather than avoid it.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made the C3 signature detail an optional choice for clients, not a default, and treated C4 client stories as a possible later chapter rather than part of the core idea.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Some clients want invisible repair, so the mark must not be imposed. Keeping C4 optional prevents the idea from depending on a second, more complex event.

final_proposal.title: Fermé pour réparations
final_proposal.idea: One day a year, Dior closes its flagship on avenue Montaigne to new sales and hangs a sign: Closed for repairs. The shop floor and windows become working ateliers where petites mains mend clients' Dior pieces in public view, including secondhand ones. Boutiques worldwide join in, so the gesture travels around the globe. The most valuable retail space in luxury is given to care instead of newness. The day is the public face of a year-round Dior repair service, launched beforehand and backed by an annual public report on what was mended. It shows craft behind the price and makes repair a house ritual, not a footnote.
follow_up_questions: What should a client leave with after their piece is mended, such as a story, a record of its life or an optional signature detail, so that repair feels like gaining something rather than fixing a loss?
Which year-round commitments would make the closure day credible rather than a stunt, and what would Dior be willing to publish about them each year?
How could the day invite people who do not own Dior, such as secondhand buyers, students or local repairers, without diluting the sense of luxury?

revisions_after_selection.change: Reframed the Slow Lane as an opt-in choice for customers, not a fixed counter. Shoppers can pick it, and staff signal availability with a simple 'Slow Lane open' sign during quieter periods.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made the creative openly own Mastercard's role in speed, with a line of copy acknowledging that Mastercard made paying faster and is now helping people use the time it saved.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This addresses the hypocrisy risk directly and turns it into the campaign's honest, distinctive point of view.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a light-touch pilot design: a handful of streets, a simple merchant kit, a staff conversation guide, and local charity partners to help staff welcome people without turning chats into scripted interventions.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Merchant willingness and staff comfort are the biggest delivery risks. A small, supported pilot tests them before scaling.

revisions_after_selection.change: Moved the Lonely Hours Map from a rival idea to an optional supporting layer, using only aggregated public or opt-in insight to help choose pilot neighbourhoods and quiet times, and kept it out of consumer-facing messaging.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It sharpens where to pilot without taking on the privacy and 'surveillance' risk of making data the headline.

revisions_after_selection.change: Defined success through merchant participation, customer feedback and conversation-based indicators, not any claim to reduce loneliness.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Spending data and footfall cannot prove loneliness impact, and overclaiming would damage credibility.

final_proposal.title: The Slow Lane
final_proposal.idea: Mastercard made paying take a fraction of a second. Now it gives some time back. Local cafés, bakeries and shops opt in to offer a Slow Lane: a signposted spot at the till with no queue pressure, a stool if there's room, and staff glad to chat. The terminal still completes the payment instantly, but the screen says 'Take your time.' It's for everyone, so nobody has to say they're lonely to use it. Mastercard owns its part in the speed story and uses it to back small businesses and the human moments around a purchase. A pilot on a few streets, with a simple merchant kit and local charity partners, can grow into a wider programme.
follow_up_questions: What would make a shop owner feel the Slow Lane is a genuine asset to their business, not an extra burden on a busy day?
How could the Slow Lane feel warm and welcoming without staff or customers feeling pressured to talk, so that quiet company counts as success too?
Beyond the till, where else has Mastercard's drive for speed removed a small human moment, and could a 'slow' option work there as well?

revisions_after_selection.change: Brought in loneliness charities as co-designers and as the destination for unclaimed rebates. They also offer a 'nobody on my list yet' route that connects people to local befriending or community groups.

element_review.selected_core_idea: Dior reveals the hidden extra inch of seam allowance inside its couture garments as a quiet promise of a long life, and frames refitting, repair and passing on as the 'next inch' of a garment's story.

candidate_elements.element: Real owners' stories of a garment's life, told through the refit of a piece they love, with the original owner present where they consent
candidate_elements.purpose: Adds the emotional core that offsets the technical dryness of the seam allowance and shows the inch at work in real lives.
candidate_elements.reason: The main concern for C2 is that the detail could feel dry. Real owners and real refits solve this. Only the owner-story element is taken from C1, not the damage-as-fashion spectacle, which risks romanticising damage and devaluing the pieces.

candidate_elements.element: Damage as a deliberate couture signature on a runway
candidate_elements.purpose: Would add provocation and press impact.
candidate_elements.reason: It conflicts with the longevity-through-craft promise, risks seeming to celebrate damage, and needs creative-director buy-in. It would pull attention away from the inch.

candidate_elements.element: Atelier hands performing each refit, credited by first name and shown in close-up
candidate_elements.purpose: Gives the inch a human face and shows who makes the promise real. It also builds trust that service capacity exists.
candidate_elements.reason: It supports the core idea as a storytelling layer. It is kept subordinate to the inch and the owner stories so that it does not become the familiar craft-hero trope.

candidate_elements.element: Owner number two: a Dior-supervised second-life pathway where a refitted piece is passed or resold to a new owner, with the next inch recorded in the garment's file
candidate_elements.purpose: Covers the reuse side of the brief with a tangible offer and shows the inch serving later owners.
candidate_elements.reason: The brief covers reuse as well as repair, and C2 only implies it. It is included as an opt-in extension, not a full resale business. Previous-owner details are kept private by default to avoid privacy and cannibalisation concerns.

candidate_elements.element: Numbered labels listing previous wearers
candidate_elements.purpose: Would make provenance a status symbol.
candidate_elements.reason: Visible owner history raises privacy concerns and would need a business-model overhaul. It is better as a later option.

candidate_elements.element: A published Dior longevity standard, covering the minimum seam allowance on couture and ready-to-wear and the equivalent repair measures for leather goods and shoes
candidate_elements.purpose: Backs the promise with verifiable commitments and reduces the greenwashing risk.
candidate_elements.reason: The credibility of the idea depends on it. It also gives a concrete way to stretch the inch to resoling, re-edging and re-strapping.

candidate_elements.element: The Inch Service: a bookable refit and repair offer, with a ribbon or tape marking the inch in each refitted piece
candidate_elements.purpose: Turns the message into behaviour and gives the campaign a repeatable touchpoint in boutiques and online.
candidate_elements.reason: The selection depends on people having something to do. A named service makes the platform operational and gives the inch a physical symbol.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added real owners' refit stories, with consent, as the emotional spine of the campaign films and content.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This directly addresses the concern that the technical detail could feel dry, and it borrows the strongest part of C1 without its risks.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added atelier hands as a supporting storytelling layer, without making craft heroes the lead.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It shows who delivers the promise and builds confidence in service capacity, while avoiding the forgettable craft-hero trope of C4.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added an opt-in 'next owner' pathway where a refitted piece can be passed on or resold through Dior, with provenance private by default.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It covers the reuse half of the brief that C2 only implied, while avoiding the privacy, exclusivity and business-model concerns of full C3.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a published longevity standard and a bookable Inch Service, with equivalents of the inch for leather goods and shoes.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It reduces greenwashing risk, extends the metaphor beyond garments, and turns the idea into behaviour.

final_proposal.title: The Extra Inch
final_proposal.idea: Inside every well-made Dior couture garment, an extra inch of seam allowance waits, so the piece can be taken in, let out and refitted across decades. The Extra Inch reveals this hidden detail as Dior's quiet promise of a long life, and treats each refit, repair or passing-on as the garment's 'next inch'. Short films follow real owners and the atelier hands who refit their pieces. A bookable Inch Service lets clients refit, repair or pass on a piece, with equivalents like resoling and re-edging for shoes and leather goods. A published longevity standard backs the promise. Luxury becomes a long relationship with a garment, not a single purchase.
follow_up_questions: What would be the most surprising way to let people see or feel the inch, such as a tape measure, a label, a ribbon or a moment of refitting, without a sustainability lecture?
How could the inch work as a promise for pieces with no seam allowance, like bags, shoes and jewellery, so it feels equally true for them?
What should happen at the moment a piece moves to its next owner, and who should get to decide how much of its history is shared?

final_proposal.title: The Slow Lane
final_proposal.idea: Mastercard made paying take a fraction of a second. Now it gives time back. In participating local shops and cafés, a marked Slow Lane offers an unhurried counter, a stool, and staff happy to chat. The terminal reads 'Take your time' while the payment still completes instantly. The campaign owns the paradox openly: speed is for when you need it, time is for when you don't. Merchants opt in with a simple kit, no scripts, and no mention of loneliness, so it's for everyone. Local community groups quietly point people towards it, and aggregate Economics Institute footfall data helps choose pilot streets. Success is judged by participation and the conversations it starts, not grand claims.

How might the Slow Lane's signature cues, such as the 'Take your time' terminal message, a sound, or the stool, become recognisable symbols that people want to share and that other brands cannot easily copy?

candidate_elements.purpose: Gives the day a tangible take-away and a recognisable visual code that can carry into editorial and social, and lets clients who want to show their piece's history do so.

candidate_elements.element: Year-round Dior repair and care service that the closure day publicly launches and points to, with clear, published commitments such as turnaround times, eligible pieces and lifetime care for the house's own products.
candidate_elements.purpose: Answers the biggest concern, that the day is dismissed as a one-day stunt, by making the day the public face of a standing offer. It also gives the visitors who join the day a way to continue the relationship afterwards.
candidate_elements.reason: The brief is about repair and reuse as behaviour, not spectacle. Without a standing service the idea would be a gesture only, and the selection already identifies this pairing as the main way to manage the stunt risk.

candidate_elements.element: Open transparency layer: a public account of the repair programme's scale and results (pieces repaired, materials reused, what Dior is doing about supply-chain practices) published after each Closed for Repairs day.
candidate_elements.purpose: Meets the scrutiny risk head on, so the gesture invites questions the brand can answer rather than looking hypocritical.
candidate_elements.reason: A luxury house closing its doors for care will be examined. Measurable, honest reporting turns that scrutiny into credibility and builds cumulative trust year on year.

candidate_elements.element: Client story wall: short stories of the pieces being mended, told in the boutique and online, with a few selected for a later showcase.
candidate_elements.purpose: Adds emotional depth and shareable content by showing why people keep and repair their pieces, and gives clients a role as co-authors of the story.
candidate_elements.reason: It is light to run and reinforces the personal, existing-owner angle of the core idea. A full runway show is excluded because it would be a second, competing event, but stories collected on the day are cheap and make the repair feel real.

candidate_elements.element: Full runway show built from clients' returned Dior pieces, reinterpreted by the ateliers.
candidate_elements.purpose: Elevates reuse as creative authorship with a major fashion-calendar moment.
candidate_elements.reason: It is a separate, large event that would dilute the simplicity of the closure day and add cost. It is better kept as a possible later chapter, as the selection noted.

candidate_elements.element: Capsule collection designed with generous seam allowances, replaceable components and lifetime alteration promises.
candidate_elements.purpose: Offers product-level proof that Dior designs for repair and long life.

candidate_elements.element: Open invitation to secondhand and resale owners, so pieces bought pre-owned can also be brought in on the day, with a clear note on how they will be authenticated.

final_proposal.title: Fermé pour réparations
final_proposal.idea: One day a year, Dior closes its flagship to new sales and hangs a sign: Closed for repairs. The shop floor and windows become working ateliers where the petites mains mend clients' own Dior pieces in public view, whether bought new or pre-owned. Boutiques worldwide join in that week. Clients can choose an invisible mend or a discreet tone-on-tone cannage signature, and their stories are told in store and online. The day launches a permanent Dior repair and care service with published commitments, and afterwards Dior reports openly on pieces repaired, materials reused and progress on its supply chain. The house's most valuable space goes to care instead of newness, proving the value of what you already own.
follow_up_questions: What would Dior have to promise publicly, such as turnaround times, lifetime care or pricing, for the repair service to feel like a real offer rather than a one-day gesture?
How could the day be designed so that people who never enter a Dior boutique, including secondhand owners and young fans of vintage Dior, feel invited and not just observers?

Which other luxury rituals, such as a seasonal sale or a store opening, could be inverted in the same way to show care instead of newness, and how might they sit alongside this day as a wider platform?

candidate_elements.element: Care-led framing in which the mend marks long ownership and careful wear, not damage, with guidance on how to look after pieces
candidate_elements.purpose: Reduces the risk of seeming to celebrate damage or discourage careful ownership.

final_proposal.title: The Cannage Darn
final_proposal.idea: Dior turns repair into a signature. The petites mains develop a hand-stitched mend based on the cannage lattice, and owners choose a visible mark or an invisible one. final_proposal.title: Tap Together
final_proposal.idea: Loneliness is hard to admit, so Tap Together lets you invite someone without asking for anything. Send a friend, neighbour, ex-colleague or relative an 'On Me' invitation to a coffee, a haircut or a bowl of noodles at a local business. The anniversary show closes with the remade pieces worn by their original owners. How should the remade pieces live after the show (exhibition, archive, back with their owners), and who should decide?

Now, each season, the ateliers invite clients to bring a treasured piece from any year: a tired Bar jacket, a worn Lady Dior, an inherited coat. candidate_elements.purpose: Helps people follow through on social plans.

candidate_elements.reason: It introduces stranger matching and the risk of pity, which the Slow Lane avoids by being open to everyone. It is also a familiar mechanic and would dilute the surprising stance.

candidate_elements.purpose: Answers merchant throughput concerns with evidence and separates a sustained movement from a stunt.

candidate_elements.purpose: Widens the lane's everyday value and reinforces that it carries no stigma.

final_proposal.title: It's Covered
final_proposal.idea: People don't only stop going out; they stop asking, because asking feels costly and like a burden. Mastercard lets any cardholder send a digital invitation to a coffee, meal or class with a simple promise: 'It's covered. Just come.' Mastercard pays for the guest's first item at participating local merchants, where owners and long-time regulars are ready to welcome newcomers. Ready-made themes (new neighbour, old friend, first one back) make the first message easy, and guests can reply privately with no obligation, then pass on an invite of their own. Launching in a few markets with caps and fraud controls, it turns Priceless into a working mechanism, brings off-peak footfall to small businesses, and is measured by invites sent, accepted and redeemed.
follow_up_questions: Which moments of life (moving to a new city, retirement, a break-up, returning to work) are the most powerful first themes for invitations, and how would each change the tone?
How could the invitation itself become a shareable, beautiful object that people are proud to send, without turning loneliness into something people have to announce?
What would make a small merchant feel like a co-author of the idea, rather than a redemption point, and what could they offer beyond the first item?
